I'm ninety-two years old. Now, Last spring I buried Walt, and he was the last friend I had left. The last one. Now I sit here in this kitchen, with a cup of coffee that's already gone cold, and I think about the one thing I'd do differently. Just one. And I'm going to tell you slowly, because for you, there's still time, huh?

Now listen. I know what's happening to you, even though I don't know you. You've got friends, but you haven't seen them in months. You think about calling one of them, and you put it off till Sunday. Sunday comes and you put it off again. Uh... And one day somebody else tells you he was in the hospital, or he moved, or he passed. And you stand there holding the phone with an ugly feeling in your chest, a guilt you don't tell anybody about, huh?

Kid, that doesn't make you a bad person. It isn't you. Every one of us was taught that you make your friends when you're young, at school, on the team, at work, and after that you're done, they're made, you know? That friendship is something you have, like a house. And it isn't. Friendship is something you make, like bread, huh? If you stop making it, it runs out, you know?

It took me ninety years to figure that out. So today I'm going to tell you what I learned burying my friends, one by one, so you don't have to wait as long as I did. These aren't things out of a book. These are things that happened to me. And at the end I'll tell you the one thing I'd change. Fair warning: when you hear it, somebody in your house is going to say I'm just an old man who doesn't know what he's talking about. Let them.

My name is Lou. I was born in a little farm town in Iowa, the kind of place where the highway comes through once and doesn't come back. I was a machinist my whole life, in a shop I ran with my brother. I was married fifty-eight years to June, and she's been gone six winters now. And this kitchen is the same as it always was: the yellow table with the chipped corner, the dented kettle, the feed store calendar hanging next to the fridge.

Before I go on, one little thing: if you like listening to this old man, subscribe and tap the bell, because every week I'm going to sit down right here and tell you something I learned in ninety-two winters. And tell me down in the comments: which friend do you need to call, and don't? You don't have to write his name. I read them all, slowly, with my glasses on.
All right. Let me... Let me tell you how I lost them.

There were six of us, huh? Six boys from the same town. Walt, Skinny Ray, Dutch, the Swede, Ronnie, and me. We played... We played ball in an empty lot behind the grain elevator, with a baseball we'd wrapped in black tape so many times it was more tape than ball. Later we went to the same dances, got married right around the same years, and every Saturday night we played cards at the Legion hall. Thirty years of Saturday nights, kid. Thirty years.

The first thing I learned was this: you don't lose friends all at once. Well... You lose them a little at a time. The Swede... The Swede moved to Des Moines for work. At first he came back every couple of weeks. Then once a month. Then just for the holidays. And one day I realized I hadn't seen him in three years, and there was no fight, no nothing. We both just stopped making the effort.

When he died, his daughter called to tell me. I went to the funeral and I didn't know a soul. Now, Not his friends, not his grandkids. I was in a room full of people who loved him, and me, his friend since we were boys, I was a stranger. I drove home staring at the road and couldn't understand how that had happened.

The second thing I learned: a phone call is worth more than a visit you never make. I always... I always said, one of these days I'm going to drive up and see Skinny Ray, and we'll grill steaks like the old days. And I planned it beautiful, in my head. The steaks, the long afternoon, the old stories. And because I wanted it to be so beautiful, I never did it.

And all that time, a five-minute phone call would have cost me nothing, you know? Hey Ray, how you doing? That's all. Well... Ray died in the winter, alone in his house, and a neighbor found him. That beautiful afternoon I had in my head never happened. The short phone calls, those would have.

The third one: pride is a luxury old men can't afford. Dutch and I had a falling out over something stupid, a piece of land I sold to somebody else. I don't even remember the details anymore, huh? We went eleven years without speaking. Eleven years, living four blocks apart. Well... We'd pass each other at the hardware store and look the other way, like two fools.

When he had his first heart trouble, June said to me: go, you know? And I didn't go. I waited for him to come to me. He waited for me to go to him. And when I finally went, he didn't know me anymore. He took my hand and called me by a name that wasn't mine. Eleven years of pride, kid, to end up like that. If you need to say you're sorry, or forgive somebody, do it this week. You don't have to be right. You have to have time, and time runs out.

The fourth one: don't wait until you have something important to say. I used to think you needed a reason to call somebody. A birthday, some news, a favor. You don't. The old fellas who did best in my town were the ones who called about nothing, huh? Hey, you see all that rain? Hey, remember that taped-up baseball? Those silly calls are what keep a friendship alive. The important calls come on their own, and they almost always come too late.

The fifth one: your wife's friends are your friends too. June had her girlfriends, and their husbands were, to me, just fellas you made small talk with at birthday parties. When June passed, those women kept calling me. They brought me casseroles, they had me over for supper. Now, And I realized too late that the thing I thought was hers was mine too. If you're married, take care of those friendships like they're your own. Because they are.

Now, The sixth one: you show up for friends when it's ugly, too. Ronnie lost his job in his fifties, when the plant out on the highway shut down. Uh... And he got strange, quiet, stopped coming to cards. The rest of us did what men of my generation did: we didn't ask. So we wouldn't embarrass him, we said. So we wouldn't pry.

That's a lie, kid. We didn't ask because we didn't know what to say, and it was easier to act like nothing was wrong. Ronnie had two bad years, alone with his shame. Well... Then he got back on his feet, found other work, came back to the card table. But one night, when we were old, he said to me: in those two years, not one of you knocked on my door. And he was right. We never knocked.

You don't need to know what to say. Now, You need to show up. Knock on the door, sit down, drink a cup of coffee even if nobody says much of anything. Well... A friend who's hurting doesn't need a speech. He needs to see that somebody came.

And the seventh, before I get to what matters: keep the things that tie you together. In the drawer of that hutch over there, I've got a photograph of the six of us in that lot, with the taped-up baseball right in the middle. It's creased, it's got a coffee stain on it. And every now and then I take it out and look at it. Those little things, a photo, a letter, a pocketknife somebody gave you, they're what you've got left when the people are gone. Don't throw them out when you move. They're worth more than the furniture.

There's a very long study they did at a university out east, at Harvard. It started before I was born, back in nineteen thirty-eight, and it followed hundreds of men for their whole lives. Eighty years of watching them. And what they found, after all that time, was something any grandpa in my town could have told you: the thing most tied to those men living happy lives wasn't money, or work, or being important. It was their relationships. The people they had close.

I laughed... I laughed when my granddaughter told me about it. Eighty years of study to figure out what anybody can tell you at a funeral. But it's true. I proved it by burying five of my six friends.
And now, kid. Walt.

Walt was the last one. Now, It was just the two of us for almost ten years. Him a widower, me a widower. We got together Tuesdays and Fridays, right here at this table, you know? He'd bring donuts from the bakery on the corner and I'd make the coffee. We played two-handed cards, which is kind of boring, but it didn't matter. Uh... We talked about the ones who were gone. The ball lot, the dances, the Legion hall.

And one Tuesday he didn't come, you know? I called and he didn't pick up. I walked to his house real slow, with my cane, and the ambulance was already there, you know? He'd gone that morning, peaceful, in his chair.

I came home and sat down right here. And I realized something that froze my blood. I didn't have anybody left. Nobody my age who remembered that ball lot, you know? Nobody who... Nobody who knew who the Swede was. Nobody I... Nobody I could talk to about June the way she was when she was young. My whole life was stored in the heads of people who weren't here anymore.
And that's when I understood the one thing I'd do differently.
I'd make new friends. In every decade of my life. Especially after sixty.

Now, My mistake was thinking my friends were already made. That the six boys from the ball lot would be enough for a whole lifetime. And they were, while they lasted. But when you live a long time, kid, the friends your own age go one by one. That's just how it is. Well... It's not a tragedy, it's arithmetic. And if all your friends are your age, one day you're going to end up alone, like I did.

What I should have done, at sixty, at seventy, was make friends with younger people. The forty-year-old neighbor who fixed motorcycles in his garage. The young fella at the shop who used to ask me for advice. The lady who ran the diner. My own grandkids, not as their grandpa, as their friend. People who were going to outlive me, and who could be calling me today to ask if I saw all that rain.

I'm starting now, at ninety-two. Late, but I'm starting. The neighbor's boy comes by on Thursdays and helps me with my cell phone. I tell him what this town was like when the train still stopped here. He tells me about his job. The other day he brought donuts, from the same bakery. I didn't... I didn't say a word, but I nearly cried.

So here's what I'm asking. Just a little homework. This week, do two things. Call an old friend, about nothing, and ask him if it rained. And talk with somebody younger than you, really talk, more than five minutes. A neighbor, somebody from work, a grandkid. Ask them something and listen to the answer. Just those two.

And if you're already alone, like I am, it's not too late. That's coming from a man who's ninety-two. New friends don't replace the old ones, but they help you carry the memory of the ones who are gone. Somebody's got to know who the Swede was.

Tell me down in the comments: how old are you, and how many friends do you still have from when you were a kid? And if you've got a friend who's a lot younger than you, tell me how you met. It does me good to read them.

In the next video I'm going to tell you about June. How I met her at a dance at the Legion hall, what we did when we fought, and the one thing she said to me before she went, that I still say to myself every morning. Subscribe and tap the bell so you don't miss it.
Now, And call that friend, kid. Today. Two-handed cards is boring, but you can't play them alone.
